title: The man who didn't know its mouth
hookLine: King Janaka meets a man who claimed to know the Gayatri and is hauling loads like an elephant. what did he miss?
carry: the gayatri's mouth is fire: it burns away wrong
tomorrow: where does Krishna say he is the Gayatri?

lines: A KING, AND A MAN WHO KNEW THE VERSE.
cards: King Janaka of Videha, well-known in the Upanishads for his wisdom, meets a man named Budila. Budila once claimed he knew the Gayatri inside out. And here he is, as the text puts it, become an elephant, hauling loads.
So the king needles him: you called yourself a knower of the Gayatri, and look at you. What went wrong? That question closes a long passage on the verse in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.
Today: what it means to really know the Gayatri.

teach.b: Before the story, the Upanishad takes the verse apart. Its first line, eight syllables, is matched by earth, sky and heaven: bhumir, antariksham, dyauh, eight syllables too.
The second by the three kinds of Vedic verse, rik, yajus and saman: the whole of sacred speech. The third by the three breaths, prana, apana and vyana: the whole of life. Worlds, words, breath.

teach.h: A FOURTH FOOT: THE SUN THAT BLAZES.
teach.b: Then a fourth foot, the visible one beyond all dust, the sun that blazes.
And the name: the Gayatri protects the gayas, the breaths, so it's called gayatri, the text says, offered as a meditation more than a dictionary entry. Budila, it seems, knew all of that.
Then comes Janaka's question, and Budila's answer, in paraphrase: great king, I didn't know its mouth.

Its mouth, the text says, is fire. Pile any amount of wood on a fire and it burns it all. In the same way, whoever knows this, whatever wrong they've done, burns it all away and comes out clean, pure, ageless, deathless.
That's the teaching under the riddle. Knowing the verse's parts isn't knowing the verse. Its mouth is fire: the Gayatri is meant to burn something away in the one who says it.
Hindu practice has long used the verse this way, to purify: offering water to the sun with it at sandhya, repeating it in japa.
One way to hear Budila's answer: you can recite a prayer for years and still carry the same loads.

teach.h: THE WORDS HAVE TO BE LET IN.
teach.b: The words have to be let in.

how: Hindus who keep sandhya offer water to the sun while saying the Gayatri, and many repeat it in japa as a cleansing; some teachers use the Upanishads' readings of it as a guide for meditation.

games.q: what does “the gayatri in context” mean?
o: a verse that counts out the days of the year
a verse whose lines hold worlds, words and breath, and whose mouth is fire
a verse that lists the names of the Vedic gods

games.q: what each line holds — tap the pairs.

s: the Upanishad says the Gayatri protects the breaths
the gayas are the breaths, it says; because it protects them, it's called gayatri.
Budila had never heard the Gayatri
he claimed to know it; what he didn't know, he says, was its mouth: fire.
the Upanishad says the Gayatri has only three feet
it names a fourth, the visible one beyond the dust: the blazing sun.

games.q: Janaka asks Budila why, knowing the Gayatri, he's hauling loads like an elephant. what does Budila say?
o: i never learned the fourth foot
i said it at the wrong hour
games.why: its mouth is fire. as fire burns all the wood you pile on, one who knows this burns away wrongdoing and comes out clean.

practice: Before you begin, name one thing you'd like burned away: a grudge, a habit, a heaviness you keep carrying. Then, if you chant, say the Gayatri slowly, or hold its meaning, may our thoughts be stirred, line by line.
Picture each line going in, not out, like wood fed into a fire. If you don't pray, simply name the weight, breathe in, out and through, and let a little of it go with each out-breath.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri in context. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, its lines hold worlds, words and breath, and its mouth is fire. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: fire; in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, fire is the Gayatri's mouth, which burns away wrongdoing.

carryVoice: Your line: the Gayatri's mouth is fire, it burns away wrong. Know the words, and let them in. I'll be here tomorrow.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.14.1–3 (the three feet of the Gayatri: earth, sky, heaven; rik, yajus, saman; prana, apana, vyana; a fourth foot, the blazing sun)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.14.4 (it protects the gayas, the breaths; therefore it is called gayatri)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.14.8 (Janaka of Videha and Budila Ashvatarashvi: 'I did not know its mouth'; its mouth is fire, and as fire burns all the wood, one who knows this burns away wrongdoing)
